If someone says something scurrilous about a person, they are making a vicious, unfair, and often vulgar attack on that person's character or reputation — usually through words, and usually in a way that is meant to humiliate, damage, or destroy how others see that person.

Think of it as criticism that has gone bad. Very, very bad.
Breaking It Down: The Two Sides of Scurrilous

The word carries two overlapping qualities at once, and both are almost always present:

1. It is defamatory. Scurrilous statements are not fair criticism. They are attacks — exaggerated, distorted, or outright false — designed to ruin someone's name or standing. The goal is not to inform or correct, but to destroy.

2. It is vulgar and coarse. The language or tone is low, crude, and tasteless. There is no dignity in it. It wallows in nastiness rather than rising above it.

When you combine those two things — vicious attack + crude, ugly delivery — you get something scurrilous.
What Makes It "Scurrilous" and Not Just "Critical"

This is important. Criticism can be honest, fair, and even harsh, and still not be scurrilous. A restaurant review that says "the food was terrible and the service was rude" is harsh, but it is not scurrilous. It is direct, proportionate, and honest.

A scurrilous attack, by contrast, has these features:

  • It is malicious. There is a mean-spirited, almost gleeful cruelty behind it. The person saying it wants to hurt.
  • It is unfair or baseless. It exaggerates wildly, twists the truth, or simply makes things up. It is not interested in accuracy — only in damage.
  • It is coarse in tone. Even if the words themselves are not swear words, the overall feel is ugly, low, and without class.
  • It targets reputation. The purpose is almost always to make others think badly of the person being attacked — to shame them publicly.

So if a political opponent releases a pamphlet full of twisted lies and degrading personal insults about a rival, designed purely to humiliate them — that pamphlet is scurrilous.

• The newspaper was sued for publishing scurrilous allegations about the politician that had no factual basis.
  • He ignored the scurrilous rumours being spread about him by jealous colleagues.
  • The pamphlet was a scurrilous attack on the general's character, full of crude insults and outright lies.
  • She was shocked by the scurrilous things he said about her in public.
  • The internet is unfortunately a breeding ground for scurrilous gossip.

Notice a pattern: scurrilous almost always involves words about a person, and those words are aimed at destroying how others see that person.

It helps to contrast it with similar words so you don't mix them up.

Not the same as "critical." Criticism can be fair and measured. Scurrilous attacks are not. They are biased, overblown, and driven by malice.

Not the same as "satirical." Satire is clever and witty. It exaggerates to make a point, and it usually contains a core of truth. Something scurrilous is not trying to be clever or truthful — it just wants to wound.

Not the same as "rude." Being rude means being impolite or disrespectful. Scurrilous goes much further — it is a full, deliberate assault on someone's reputation.

Not the same as "vulgar" alone. Something can be vulgar (crude, indecent) without being scurrilous. A dirty joke is vulgar but not scurrilous. Scurrilous requires a target — a person being attacked and dragged through the mud.

Scurrilous is a strong word. It is not something you would use to describe everyday rudeness or a mildly unfair comment. You use it when the attack is really nasty — when it goes beyond the boundaries of decent discourse and enters the territory of deliberate character assassination delivered in a low, ugly way.

On a scale of intensity, think of it like this:

Unflattering → Critical → Harsh → Cutting → Scathing → Scurrilous

By the time you reach scurrilous, you are at the far end — where attacks are not just sharp but dirty, dishonest, and cruel.
Words That Often Appear Alongside It

In real usage, you will often see "scurrilous" paired with these words:

  • Scurrilous allegations — false or exaggerated accusations meant to shame
  • Scurrilous rumours — nasty gossip designed to destroy someone's name
  • Scurrilous attack — a vicious, degrading assault on someone's character
  • Scurrilous language — coarse, abusive speech aimed at demeaning someone
  • Scurrilous campaign — an organized effort to destroy someone's reputation through ugly means
A Simple Way to Remember It

Picture a tabloid newspaper from centuries ago — one of those nasty, gossipy sheets full of twisted lies, crude insults, and scandalous accusations about famous people. The kind of writing that was designed to shock, to humiliate, and to ruin people — not to inform.

That is scurrilous. Loud, dirty, unfair, and aimed straight at someone's good name.

If it's cruel, it's coarse, it's false or grossly exaggerated, and it's designed to make the world think less of someone — it's scurrilous.
